blocks.text: A column can look completely numeric, full of values that print exactly like numbers, and still be stored as plain text underneath. Every arithmetic operation on it will fail or misbehave, every plot that touches it will break or plot nonsense, and none of this announces itself with an obvious error. It just quietly produces wrong answers until someone happens to look closely. Catching this is not a formatting nicety, it is one of the most consequential checks in the entire cleaning process.
1. Why Wrong Data Types Happen Constantly

CSV files, and most other plain text formats, have no real type system built in. Every single value in a CSV is just a string of characters. When pandas reads a CSV with read_csv, it has to guess what each column actually represents by scanning the values in it, and that guess can be wrong or overly conservative.

The scary part is how little it takes to break the guess. If a numeric column has 999 rows that look like clean numbers and one row that contains something like the string "N/A", pandas cannot store 999 numbers and one string in the same array, a numpy array is strictly one dtype for the whole column. So pandas falls back to storing the ENTIRE column as an object dtype, which is really just a column of Python strings. All 999 genuinely numeric looking values silently become text too, just because of one stray row.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

data = {"price": ["19.99", "24.50", "N/A", "12.00"]}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df["price"].dtype)   # object, not float64, because of that one "N/A"

blocks.text: 2. Detecting the Problem

Before converting anything, you need to know which columns are already wrong. This detection pass should be automatic, something you run on every new dataset before any other cleaning step touches it.
2.1 df.dtypes as the First Check

df.dtypes prints the dtype pandas settled on for every column in one line. This should be the very first thing you look at after loading any new dataset. An object dtype on a column you expect to hold numbers, like price, quantity, or age, is an immediate red flag.

code.content:
print(df.dtypes)
# price        object    <- should be float64, something is wrong
# quantity      int64
# order_date   object    <- should be datetime64, not yet converted

blocks.text: 2.2 Inspecting the Actual Mix of Types
dtypes only tells you the column level verdict. When a column looks suspicious, running apply(type) across its values shows you the real mix of Python types hiding inside it.

If that output shows a mix instead, mostly str but with a handful of float or NoneType mixed in, you know exactly why pandas gave up on a numeric dtype, and you can decide how to fix it with real information instead of a guess.
3. Converting to Numeric with pd.to_numeric()

pd.to_numeric() is the standard tool for turning a column of number looking strings into an actual int64 or float64 series. It tries to parse every value, and its errors parameter controls exactly what happens the moment it hits a value that cannot be parsed.
3.1 The errors Parameter, Value by Value
There are three possible values, and picking the right one matters a great deal for what happens to your data.

blocks.content: {"headers":["errors value","behavior"],"rows":[["'raise' (the default)","Throws a ValueError the instant it hits the first value it cannot parse, stopping the whole conversion. Useful when you want to be forced to notice bad data immediately rather than have it slide through unnoticed."],["'coerce'","Converts every value it can parse normally, and turns every value it cannot parse into NaN instead of failing. This is the most common practical choice, because it lets the conversion finish and then you handle the resulting NaNs deliberately with the missing value techniques from earlier in this course."],["'ignore'","Returns the original input completely unconverted, including the values that could have parsed cleanly, the moment it hits even one value it cannot parse. One bad value can silently prevent the entire column from being converted at all, which is why this is rarely the right choice, and why recent pandas versions have deprecated it in favor of wrapping errors='raise' in your own try or except."]]}

code.content:
prices = pd.Series(["19.99", "24.50", "N/A", "12.00"])

pd.to_numeric(prices, errors="raise")     # raises ValueError the moment it hits "N/A"
pd.to_numeric(prices, errors="coerce")    # 19.99, 24.50, NaN, 12.00
pd.to_numeric(prices, errors="ignore")    # returns the four original strings, untouched

blocks.title: Coercing does not fix anything by itself
blocks.content: errors='coerce' just turns bad values into NaN, it does not decide what those missing values should become. You still need a deliberate follow up step, dropping those rows, filling them with a sensible default, or investigating why they were not numeric in the first place, using the missing value techniques from the earlier lesson in this course.

blocks.text: 4. Converting to Datetime with pd.to_datetime()

Dates and times are almost always loaded as plain strings too, and pd.to_datetime() is the function that turns those strings into real datetime64 objects, ones pandas can do date arithmetic, sorting, and resampling on correctly.

By default pandas tries to infer the date format automatically by scanning the values, and it genuinely does a good job most of the time. But automatic inference can guess wrong on ambiguous formats, for example it can flip day and month on a date like 03/04/2024, and it is noticeably slower on large files because it has to work harder to figure out the pattern first.
4.1 Pinning Down the format Parameter
Passing format explicitly removes the guessing entirely, telling pandas exactly what pattern to expect, which is both faster and immune to misinterpretation.

code.content:
df["order_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["order_date"], format="%d/%m/%Y")

# %d day, %m month, %Y four digit year, %H:%M:%S for a time component
df["order_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["order_date"], format="%d/%m/%Y %H:%M:%S")

blocks.text: On a file with millions of rows, giving to_datetime an explicit format can be dramatically faster than letting it infer, since inference has to repeatedly test candidate patterns before it can confirm which one actually fits the whole column.
5. Casting Directly with .astype()

.astype() is the general purpose tool for direct, straightforward type casts, useful when you already know exactly what type a column should become and do not need to handle unparseable values along the way.
5.1 Downsizing Numeric Types to Save Memory

pandas defaults to int64 and float64 for numeric columns, which is far more precision and range than most real columns need. An ages column, for instance, never needs the roughly 9 quintillion value range that int64 provides, a much smaller int type covers it comfortably while using a fraction of the memory.

code.content:
df["age"] = df["age"].astype("int32")     # or int16 if the range allows it
df["price"] = df["price"].astype("float32")

blocks.text: 5.2 category dtype for Low Cardinality Strings

When a string column only has a small number of distinct repeated values relative to its length, something like a country column with 300000 rows but only 40 distinct country names, category dtype stores each unique value once and represents every row as a small integer code pointing back to it. This is a real memory optimization technique, not just a formatting choice, and it also speeds up groupby and value_counts operations on that column, since pandas can work with the compact integer codes instead of repeatedly comparing full strings.
6. Worked Example: Cleaning a price Column
Say a price column comes in exactly like this, four rows, three that look like clean numbers and one contaminated with the string "unknown".
Running pd.to_numeric with errors="coerce" parses every genuinely numeric looking string cleanly and turns just the one bad value into NaN, leaving the rest of the data intact.

code.content:
df["price"] = pd.to_numeric(df["price"], errors="coerce")
print(df)
#    price
# 0  19.99
# 1    NaN
# 2  24.50
# 3  12.00

print(df["price"].dtype)   # float64

blocks.text: The column is now genuinely numeric. df["price"].sum(), .mean(), and any comparison using < or > will all work correctly, and the one row that could not be parsed is now an explicit, visible NaN instead of a silent string sitting inside a text column.
7. Why the Right Type Matters, Beyond Avoiding Errors

It is tempting to think of type conversion as just about avoiding crashes, but the wrong dtype causes damage even when nothing throws an exception. A numeric column stored as text cannot be summed, averaged, or compared with less than or greater than correctly. pandas will either refuse outright or, worse, silently do a string comparison instead of a numeric one, where "9" is considered greater than "10" because it compares character by character.

code.content:
prices_as_text = pd.Series(["9", "10", "2"])
print(prices_as_text.sort_values())
# 0     9
# 2     2
# 1    10
# sorted alphabetically, not numerically, because the dtype is still object

blocks.text: The memory and speed cost is just as real. A category dtype on a low cardinality string column can cut the memory that column uses dramatically, and that saving compounds directly into faster groupby operations, since pandas groups on the small integer codes instead of repeatedly hashing and comparing long strings.
7.1 Measuring It: memory_usage() Before and After
The saving is easy to see directly rather than take on faith. Comparing df.memory_usage() on the same column before and after converting it to category dtype shows exactly how much was recovered.

code.content:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

n = 200_000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "country": np.random.choice(["India", "USA", "UK", "Germany", "Japan"], size=n)
})

before = df.memory_usage(deep=True)["country"]
df["country"] = df["country"].astype("category")
after = df.memory_usage(deep=True)["country"]

print(f"before: {before / 1_000_000:.2f} MB")
print(f"after:  {after / 1_000_000:.2f} MB")
# before: 12.62 MB
# after:  0.20 MB

blocks.title: deep=True matters here
blocks.content: memory_usage() without deep=True does not actually measure the memory a plain object column of Python strings uses, it only counts the pointer array, which massively understates the real number. Pass deep=True whenever you are comparing string heavy columns like this, otherwise the before number will look artificially small and the improvement will look far less dramatic than it actually is.

blocks.text: 8. Common Mistakes
8.1 Coercing Silently and Never Checking the Damage

errors="coerce" is convenient precisely because it does not stop and complain, but that convenience is exactly what makes it dangerous. If a format assumption is wrong, for instance a date column where most rows use one format and a chunk of rows use another, coerce can quietly convert a large fraction of a column to NaN in a single line, and nothing about the code will look wrong. Always check df["col"].isna().sum() immediately after a coerce conversion and compare it to the count before, a big jump means something is actually broken, not just a few genuinely bad values.

code.content:
before_na = df["price"].isna().sum()
df["price"] = pd.to_numeric(df["price"], errors="coerce")
after_na = df["price"].isna().sum()
print(f"conversion introduced {after_na - before_na} new missing values")

blocks.text: 8.2 Downsizing an Int Type Without Checking the Range First

int8 holds values from -128 to 127, int16 from -32768 to 32767, and so on. Casting a column to a smaller int type without first checking whether any value in it actually exceeds that range does not raise a clean error, it silently wraps around and produces a completely wrong number sitting quietly in your data.

code.content:
values = pd.Series([100, 200, 50])
print(values.astype("int8"))
# 0    100
# 1    -56    <- 200 overflowed and wrapped around silently, not an error, just wrong
# 2     50

blocks.text: Before downsizing, check the actual min and max of the column against the target type's range, or use pd.to_numeric with downcast="integer", which inspects the real values first and only downcasts as far as it can safely go.

code.content:
print(df["age"].min(), df["age"].max())    # confirm this actually fits the target type first
df["age"] = pd.to_numeric(df["age"], downcast="integer")

blocks.text: 9. A Systematic Type Conversion Checklist
A quick, repeatable pass over a new dataset catches almost every type problem before it has a chance to cause damage further down the pipeline.

items: Run df.dtypes right after loading, before doing anything else, and flag every column whose dtype does not match what it logically should be.
For any suspicious object column, run df["col"].apply(type).value_counts() to see the real mix of Python types hiding inside it.
Convert numeric looking columns with pd.to_numeric(errors="coerce"), then immediately check isna().sum() before and after to confirm the number of new missing values is small and expected.
Convert date looking columns with pd.to_datetime(), passing an explicit format whenever the default inference is ambiguous or the file is large.

Before casting numeric columns to a smaller int or float type with astype, check the column's actual min and max against the target type's range, or use pd.to_numeric with downcast="integer" instead of guessing.
Cast low cardinality string columns to category dtype, and confirm the memory saving with df.memory_usage(deep=True) before and after.
Re run df.dtypes one last time at the end of the pass to confirm every column landed on the type it was actually supposed to.
